Capricorn One (1977) is my go to for "retro" films that anyone can watch

Takes the well known conspiracy about the moon landing, slightly adjusts it to be about Mars in a hypothetical 70s where people have lost interest in space exploration, and goes with it 110% further. How would an organisation like NASA  (with the support of state departments like FBI/CIA) be able to hide the reality that the launch couldn't be completed safely? 

The rocket is launched without the astronauts in it, who are then sent off to a remote military base in the desert where they act out a landing on Mars and even call back to earth to speak with their adoring wives, having to lie about their experiences. Or do they? The movie has several "Tarantino" crazy action and thriller like scenes of the many characters trying to unravel the conspiracy. A technitian who notices something off about the telemetry signals is disappeared by the CIA and his journalist friend desperately tries to find evidence that he ever existed, and the atronauts try to escape back to society through the american desert...

My absolute favourite scene, that has that crazy monologue  style of tarantino, is when one astronaut climbs a cliff face, telling a long winded joke about how to break bad news about a cat falling off a roof....

The practical stunts by the helicopters hunting the astronauts are incredible feats, and unfortunately resulted in the death of one of the pilots. An achievement of cinema that according to the pilot's family should be honoured.

It has all the hallmarks of a good cult film while still having intrigue and action that keeps people used to block busters intrigued

I work in Market Researce. Focus testing films is one of the things my firm does.

These movies were the most liked by focus groups in my 15 years of experience. About 98% of participants (Base N 100 per market, 10 markets) enjoyed;

Sing 2, Frozen, Top Gun Maverick, Avengers Endgame, The Help, American Sniper, Coco, Spider-Man: No Way Home, The Blindside, The Green Book, Zootopia, Up, Incredibles 2, The Passion of the Christ, Black Panther, and The Wonder. 

I have yet to see a film tested by audiences recieve a 100% approval rating. But all the ones I mentioned were 98-99% approval, especially the animated films Up, Zootopia, Sing 2, and Frozen. Elemental was also very highly rated, but I didn't work directly on that focus group testing.

Audiences are willing to give violence a pass most of the time. Sex is the no-go generally. Historical drama with a stronger protagonist and moralistic perspective is audience gold- Gladiator is one of the highest-tested films I have ever seen. 

People may trash-talk superhero films, ("hate on the Avengers" I am not sure what this all entails), but they are crowd-pleasers to a large degree. The first Avengers and Endgame films were extremely well-liked. 

I am not sure if any film would get a perfect 100% approval rating. At least I have never seen such. Though I think the Avengers and Gladiator would get really close. 

The only documentaries I have seen test well are long-form true crime docs that are specifically about non-African American missing or murdered women (kids are a no-go in this genre) and biopics about controversial celebrities. Nature documentaries are typically "indifferent" on the overall audience score card. 

I wouldn't bet on a Nature doc, ever.
I despise that people love The Help, The Blindside and The Green Book. I wonder how diverse these focus groups are.

Understandable. 

General audiences don't return to movies too often. Which is worth keeping in mind. A lot of folks just see 2-3 big movies a year in most markets and only a handful of US cities actually drive the majority of the entertainment film industry. 

So that's how we get movies like Endgame or Avatar making ridiculous money and also being regarded so highly by audiences in part. 

People LOVE those Avatar films and it's the damnest thing to my own sensibilities. But they are essentially, "perfectly" made films for a majority of movie watchers.

Extremely diverse. We are required to get a very broad cross-section of race, gender, income, and marital status.

Mainstream films are expressly created to appeal to as broad an audience as possible and offend the least number of people. They will recut and reshoot most of a film if it bombs with any required demographic. 

Studios send a proposal to research firms that outline all the demographics required to screen the film. Meaning the firm has to recruit these quotas expressly by %. 

For example, we would need to recruit a minimum of 62% Caucasian, 13% African American, 20% Hispanic/Latino, etc. 50% Females 18-35, etc.

Focus testing goes through "rounds". A film isn't screened once for a given set of demos and never again. You test it again and again with a big cross-section of folks.  

The Fast and Furious franchise is, for example, one of the best-testing franchises of all time. Because the demographic requirements are so exhaustive. The filmmakers do a lot to ensure that the franchise appeals to almost everyone.

I think this premise probably works in age groups. There’s films that people currently aged 30-50 would all like, but those aren’t the same films that the 15-29 crowd might like. There will always be outliers and overlap at the transition from one age group to another, but if you take a 20 year old and a 35 year old right now it’s going to be very different.

Young people now especially have a vastly different world view and tend to view things through a current social lens. I disagree with that principle sometimes, and I think that films should be evaluated in context to when they were made, but it doesn’t change the fact that a lot of young people evaluate this way. When you look at things that way, a LOT of stuff comes up as ‘problematic’ and gets written off by this group. 

On the other hand, I personally find new films catering to today’s pop culture disinteresting - I hated Bodies Bodies Bodies.
